transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-07 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (QuantaHealth ML Eng), Ravi Sharma (QuantaHealth Platform Eng), Dr. Elena Ruiz (CTO), Priya Menon (SRE)

Summary:
Quick sync to review last week's pilot numbers after we changed concurrency ceiling and lowered max batch wait to 20ms. Focus: smoothing burst behavior, tail p50/p95/p99 shifts, and whether continuous batching is causing head-of-line delays for small requests.

Topics:
- Recent benchmark summary (12-hour rolling windows)
- Continuous batching config and tradeoffs
- Concurrency targets, per-GPU queueing/backpressure
- KV cache hit rate impact on end-to-end throughput
- Autoscale & burst capacity policies
- Next steps + owners

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: alright hi everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh we're on the 15th minute slot so i'll go quick. Samir from Redwood here, with Lena. How are you folks?
[00:07] Maya: hey, good thanks. Quick note, we had some noisy logs in the last run, so there might be gaps in the traces we uploaded.
[00:13] Lena: noted, that's fine, we can work with partial traces. Quick agenda, run through numbers, dig into the p95 spikes, propose two config changes and agree next steps.
[00:22] Ravi: sound good. We're eager, tail latency is killing the UX at peak.
[00:27] Dr. Elena: hi, i only have the first 20 minutes, just to hear whether this is trending in the right direction.

[00:40] Samir: cool. So quick recap — last week we bumped the concurrency ceiling from 64 to 96 per node and lowered the max batch delay from 50ms to 20ms to prioritize latency over micro-batching. The result: p50 improved by ~10%, p95 down by 15% except during burst windows where p99 spiked.
[01:02] Maya: yeah we saw that, but the p99 spikes were weird — seemed correlated with a particular traffic pattern where we get ~600 small requests over 10s.
[01:12] Lena: that's classic head-of-line; continuous batching will try to pack those requests which helps throughput but can add latency for the small ones. You can think of it like a train waiting to fill up.
[01:23] Priya: is there a way to prioritize small requests? The product team wants snappy replies for interactive flows.
[01:29] Lena: yes, two levers — batch sizing thresholds and request bucketing. We can set a low-latency lane where max wait is 5-10ms and a throughput lane with 50-100ms. 
[01:40] Ravi: what about concurrency? we saw GPU utlization drop at certain points when batching was aggressive.
[01:46] Samir: that's likely because the KV cache hit rate fluctuated — when cache hits are high, per-request work is smaller, so batching becomes less efficient and GPUs idle more between big batches.
[01:58] Maya: our KV hit rate is about 72% average but drops to ~40% during cold starts. Could that explain the p99 behavior?
[02:06] Lena: absolutely, cold cache -> larger compute per request -> longer queues -> tail spikes. We proposed a pre-warm policy in the pilot playbook, but we didn't enable it in your run.
[02:18] Dr. Elena: ok so enabling pre-warm might smooth the spikes. How risky is that for cost?
[02:24] Samir: small incremental cost — you keep a fraction of GPU hot as a warm pool. Alternatively, you can use burst capacity which bills only when used but requires a few extra setup steps.
[02:36] Maya: on the burst capacity, our finance team flagged that as a procurement step, so prefer solution that stays within reserved pool if possible.
[02:44] Lena: understood. We can propose an autoscale policy that uses reserved capacity plus small buffer and a rate limiter to keep cost predictable.

[03:02] [Lena shares link: https://redwood.app/s/qt-health/batch-tuning-v1 (shared doc)]
[03:07] Lena: i've dropped the tuned batch config in the doc. Items of note: lower batch max_wait for low-latency lane (8ms), keep throughput lane at 40ms, concurrency cap at 88 for this instance type, and enable a small KV pre-warm window of 30s after cold starts.
[03:23] Ravi: ok, the concurrency cap you recommend is 88 — was that calculated from the GPU profile we sent?
[03:29] Lena: yes, we used your sequence length and token distribution to simulate. The 88 target minimizes tail without killing throughput.
[03:36] Priya: how does this interact with backpressure? during the last run we saw a growing queue and then a sudden drop when requests were rejected.
[03:43] Samir: that's retry storms and backoff mismatches. If the client retries aggressively on 429s you'll amplify bursts. We recommend client side jittered exponential backoff and a soft-throttle window on the server that returns 202-ish or 429 with Retry-After when saturating.
[04:01] Maya: our current client doesn't jitter; i'll add that to the task list.

[04:18] [00:04:18] Lena: a quick demo of the per-route dashboard — see the per-token cost and queue depth charts. At 14:40 in your run the queue depth hit 310ms average which corresponds with the p99 spike.
[04:33] Ravi: 310ms queue depth, got it. Do you have an easy way to correlate that with specific requests? the traces were a bit sparse this time.
[04:41] Lena: trace ids are in the logs we asked you to ship. Even if they're sparse, sampling at 5% should give us the tail patterns.

[05:02] Dr. Elena: can you also explain fallback to smaller model — like if we lose capacity, do we degrade gracefully?
[05:08] Samir: yes, Redwood supports automatic fallback to a cheaper, smaller model variant. You can configure policy: latency-first will fall back immediately at threshold, or throughput-first will queue briefly. We usually recommend a 2-tier fallback: 1) same model lower precision quantized variant, 2) smaller model.
[05:25] Maya: any obvious quality regressions when we go to quantized variant?
[05:29] Lena: small for generation completions in your prompts, we ran evals on your prompt set — ROUGE/RL metrics drop ~2-3% in edge cases, generally acceptable for suggestions but not for final copy.

[06:01] Samir: ok proposed action: for the next 12h stress run — 1) apply the low-latency lane (8ms), 2) concurrency cap 88, 3) enable KV pre-warm, 4) client-side jittered backoff, 5) no burst capacity for now. We'll look at p50/p95/p99 and queue depth every 2 hours.
[06:20] Ravi: we'll run that tonight. Also we'll monitor network egress to confirm no infra caps.
[06:26] Priya: one question — are there any changes to audit/logging when you enable pre-warm? compliance wants to be sure nothing hits PHI storage accidentally.
[06:35] Lena: no change to audit logs; pre-warm just populates KV namespace with safe synthetic keys you provide. We avoid real PHI. We'll set the pre-warm dataset to sanitized tokens.
[06:47] Dr. Elena: good. Also please make sure the KMS access pattern is logged.

[07:02] Maya: quick oddity — during one spike we saw a CPU process pegged on the node handling batching. Is batching CPU-bound in our setup?
[07:11] Lena: sometimes the batching controller (python shim) handles request assemble/disassemble and can be CPU-heavy if serialization is bad. We can swap to a compiled path for the shim which reduces CPU overhead. We'll include that in the config.
[07:24] Samir: agreed, include the compiled batching shim flag in the config Lena shares.

[07:34] [07:34] Lena: i've also noted a rule to split traffic by route size — short requests take lane A, long ones lane B; that dramatically reduces head-of-line blocking.
[07:45] Maya: sounds good. We'll annotate routes tomorrow.

[08:05] Priya: one more operational ask — can you add an alert when queue depth exceeds 200ms for more than 60s? we want to know before users complain.
[08:14] Samir: yes, Redwood Console supports that; we'll add a suggested alert policy in the dashboard share.

[08:26] Lena: ok to recap next steps quickly?
[08:29] Samir: recap: Lena will drop the tuned batch config, compiled shim flag, and autoscale suggestion by EOD 4/8. Maya will run the 12h stress run and share logs by 4/9. Ravi will validate egress/capacity and report any infra constraints by 4/10. Team schedules follow-up 4/12 10am PST.
[08:44] Dr. Elena: that's fine, i need the outcome of the 12-hour run; prioritize the p99 and compliance notes.

[08:55] Maya: quick question: do you recommend we enable slow-start for autoscale?
[08:59] Lena: yes, a small slow-start (30-60s) avoids immediate overprovisioning and lets the controller observe load before adding many replicas. It's a balance but reduces cost surprises.

[09:12] Samir: alright thank you everyone, we'll follow up with the documents. Any final quick Qs?
[09:18] Ravi: none. Thanks.
[09:20] Priya: thanks.
[09:22] Dr. Elena: thanks, gotta run.
[09:25] Samir: bye.

End transcript. Attachments/links referenced during call: https://redwood.app/s/qt-health/batch-tuning-v1, Shared spreadsheet: https://drive.company/QH-pilot-benchmarks, Security note: https://redwood.app/s/security/enterprise-snapshot.pdf
